title: Using the GitLab API Without Hand-Written Auth Code
summary: GitLab API provides REST and GraphQL endpoints with token authentication. You can select your auth approach and understand rate-limiting for integrations.
body_markdown:
## Frequently asked questions


After the first call works, a few questions keep coming up, and GitLab's docs answer each of them. The token you set up earlier covers most of what you'll do.


### Is the GitLab API free to use?


Yes, the API itself carries no separate charge, and it's available on GitLab's free tier as well as the paid ones. What changes by plan is the set of features behind the endpoints.


When a call works on a colleague's paid group, it can still return an error on your free one, because GitLab's docs mark some endpoints as limited to certain tiers.


Check the tier note at the top of each endpoint's docs page before you build on it, not after.


### Can I use the GitLab API on a self-managed instance?


Yes, the same REST and GraphQL APIs run on a self-managed instance, with your own host in place of gitlab.com. The catch is that the limits stop being GitLab's and become your administrator's.


If you tuned a script against gitlab.com, it may be throttled harder, or not at all, on your server, because rate limits, pagination behavior and token policies can all be configured per instance.


Ask the administrator what's set, because the public documentation only tells you the defaults.


Read the docs version that matches your instance, because its version also decides which endpoints exist.


### Should I use REST or GraphQL?


Use REST when you want a simple, predictable call for a known resource, and GraphQL when you need related data in one round trip.


REST is the better default for scripts and automations: each endpoint does one thing, and the docs show an example for it.


When you'd otherwise chain several REST calls to assemble one view, GraphQL earns its place, since you ask for exactly the fields you need.


The cost is that GraphQL enforces its own complexity limit on each query, so an ambitious query can be rejected even when your request rate is fine.


Not every feature has a counterpart in both, so check the docs for the one you need.


### How long do GitLab access tokens last?


It depends on the token type, and the expiry is the thing that will break your integration at the worst moment.


Personal, project and group access tokens are issued with an expiration date, and when it passes they stop working with a plain authentication error, not a warning.


Short-lived by design, OAuth access tokens are renewed with a refresh token, so your code has to handle that renewal.


Put each token's expiry date in your calendar when you create it. If you hand the work to a builder that manages auth for you, it handles OAuth renewal, but you still own replacing a static token before it lapses.
